junction.name: Delancey Street & Bowery, New York City

claims.text: Delancey Street & Bowery had 20 injury crashes in police records since 2021-10-31: 9 pedestrians injured, 2 cyclists injured and 0 people killed.
These counts are Delancey Street & Bowery's own: the city's record places 51 of the 140 records within 100 m at another intersection or street, and they are left out.
At the U.S. DOT's values that harm costs about $1.4 million a year.
45% of crashes here had “driver inattention/distraction” recorded as a contributing factor, against 27% at the city's priority junctions.

Held up on later years: “driver inattention/distraction” was recorded in 54% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 26% at the city's priority junctions (found by the greedy search and the exhaustive search).

The city's Leading Pedestrian Interval signals: passed the causal gate (pedestrian injury crashes changed -17% (95% interval -22% to -11%) at 1,651 sites against sites treated later or the citywide trend, and a placebo date shows nothing).
The city's turn traffic calming: earlier trend (a simple before/after says -26%, but a placebo date before the work shows a drop too, so the decline cannot be credited to the program).
The city's enhanced crossings: not shown (at 96 sites the change in pedestrian injury crashes (-7%, 95% interval -50% to +69%) could be zero).
The city's speed humps: not shown (at 1,008 sites the change in injury crashes (+0%, 95% interval -9% to +9%) could be zero).
Leading Pedestrian Interval would avoid about 0.2 crashes a year (CMF 9918, the record FHWA's fact sheet cites; evidence: the city's own past installs passed the causal gate), worth $71,000 a year.

Backplates with Retroreflective Borders would avoid about 0.6 crashes a year (CMF 1410, the record FHWA's fact sheet cites; evidence: only if a site check confirms it), worth $205,000 a year; check on site: an entry on yellow or red.
The NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is responsible for Delancey Street, Bowery (not listed in NYSDOT Roadway Inventory, so a city street).
Who can push for it: Council Member, District 1, New York City Council; Manhattan Community Board 2.
A request letter to the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is ready to draft from these facts.
